MODULES.title: Meet Claude — and where it lives
MODULES.tag: One AI, several front doors: Chat, Cowork, and Code
MODULES.why: Most people meet Claude through a single chat window and assume that's all there is. It isn't. The exact same intelligence shows up in a few different places, called surfaces, and each one is shaped for a different kind of work. Once you know the surfaces exist and roughly what each is for, you stop forcing every task through the chat box, and you start reaching for the one that actually fits. This first lesson is just the lay of the land, the map you'll use for the rest of the course.
MODULES.mental: Picture Claude as one very capable colleague who can show up in different rooms of your workspace. In the Chat room, you sit across the desk and go back and forth, you ask, it answers, you ask again. In the Cowork room, you hand off a whole job and let your colleague go work on it across your files and tools, then come back with a finished result. In the Code room, that same colleague rolls up their sleeves inside actual software. Same colleague, same smarts, three rooms. Knowing which room you're in is the whole game: you don't change who you're talking to, you change how much you hand over and how much you stay hands-on.
concepts: Surface

A place where you use Claude. There are three main ones, Chat, Cowork, and Code, plus a couple of smaller ones. They share the same underlying intelligence; what changes is how you work with it and how much it does on its own.
Chat (claude.ai and the apps)

The familiar back-and-forth window, on the web, the desktop app, and your phone. You ask, it answers, you steer every step. Best for questions, thinking something through, drafting, and looking at a file or image you upload.
Cowork

A mode in the Claude desktop app where you describe a finished deliverable once, then let Claude go do the work on its own, across folders you allow it to touch, the web, and tools you connect. It comes back with the actual thing: a formatted document, a built-out spreadsheet, a research summary. Made for non-coders.
Code (Claude Code)

The surface for building and changing real software. It lives in places engineers work, a terminal, code editors, and more. You don't need it to get value from Claude; if you're not living in a terminal, Cowork is the friendlier path to the same kind of hands-off help.
Same brain, different front doors

Cowork and Code actually run on the same hands-off engine under the hood, Cowork is just that engine made simple for everyday knowledge work. So the choice between surfaces isn't about which one is 'smarter', it's about which one fits how you want to work.
You're always in control

No matter the surface, the important calls stay with you. In Chat you drive every turn. In Cowork and Code, Claude works on its own but checks in on big decisions and lets you interrupt, redirect, or stop it at any point.
mistakes: Assuming the chat window is the only way to use Claude, there are whole surfaces built for handing off finished work, not just asking questions
Thinking Cowork or Code is 'more advanced Chat', they're a different way of working (hand off the job) not a smarter version of the same back-and-forth
Believing Code is only for programmers and writing off the hands-off surfaces entirely, Cowork gives non-coders the same kind of autonomous help
Worrying that a hands-off surface will run wild, you can watch it, redirect it, and stop it, and it pauses for the consequential decisions
Trying to force a big multi-step job through plain Chat one message at a time, when a hand-off surface would just do the whole thing
flags: "I keep copy-pasting between Claude and my files for one task", that's a sign the job wants Cowork, where Claude touches the files itself
"This is just a quick question or a quick draft", that's Chat's home turf; no need for anything fancier
"Everyone says I need Claude Code but I don't write code", you probably want Cowork, the friendly hands-off surface for non-coders
"I'm nervous about letting AI loose on my stuff", good instinct; the hands-off surfaces keep you in the loop and let you stop them anytime
ask: Am I asking a question or thinking out loud (Chat), or handing off a whole job to be finished for me (Cowork or Code)?
Does this task need Claude to actually touch my files, my browser, or a connected tool, or just talk with me?
If it's a hand-off, am I a coder working in software (Code) or a knowledge worker with documents and spreadsheets (Cowork)?
Do I know I can interrupt, redirect, or stop a hands-off surface at any time, so I can let it run without worry?

MODULES.title: The Decision: Chat vs Cowork vs Code
MODULES.tag: Two questions tell you which surface to reach for, every time
MODULES.why: This is the most useful lesson in the course, the one you'll actually run in your head before every task. There's a simple way to decide which surface fits, and it comes straight from Anthropic's own framing. Get this decision right and everything feels smooth: quick things stay quick, big things get handled, and you never feel like you're fighting the tool. Get it wrong and even simple work turns into a slog. So we're going to make the choice almost automatic.
MODULES.mental: Two questions decide it nearly every time. First: is there a clear deliverable, an actual thing you want produced and finished? Second: does the work touch your files, your browser, or your tools? If the answer to both is yes, you've got a job to hand off, reach for Cowork (or Code if you live in software). If it's really a one-off question, or you just want a thinking partner to bounce ideas off, that's Chat. As Anthropic frames it: reach for Chat when you have a one-off question or want a thought partner; reach for Cowork when there's a clear deliverable and the work touches your files or tools. Memorize those two sentences and you've basically got the whole module.
concepts: The deliverable question

Ask: is there a specific finished thing I want at the end, a built spreadsheet, a formatted report, a folder of renamed files? A clear deliverable points toward a hand-off surface. A loose 'help me think' or 'what do you reckon' points toward Chat.
The touch-my-stuff question

Ask: does getting this done require working across my actual files, folders, browser, or connected tools? If yes, you want a surface that can reach those things and act (Cowork or Code), not just talk about them (Chat).
Reach for Chat when...

You have a one-off question, want to think something through, need a draft or a rewrite, or want to analyze a single file or image you upload. You stay in the driver's seat, steering each turn. It's quick, conversational, and where most people spend most of their time.
Reach for Cowork when...

There's a clear deliverable and the work spans your files, your browser, or your tools. You describe the finished result once, and Claude goes and produces it, working across everything you've allowed, then hands it back. It's the move for 'go make this whole thing for me.'
Reach for Code when...

You're building or changing real software in an actual codebase, and you're comfortable in developer tools like a terminal or code editor. It runs on the same hands-off engine as Cowork, just aimed at software work. If you're not a coder, that same power is waiting for you in Cowork.
When in doubt, start in Chat

If you genuinely can't tell, start a conversation in Chat. It's the lowest-friction surface, and Claude can help you figure out whether your task is actually a hand-off job. You can always graduate to Cowork once the deliverable becomes clear.
mistakes: Defaulting to Chat for a big multi-file job and then copy-pasting forever, that's exactly the deliverable-plus-touches-your-files pattern that wants Cowork
Reaching for a hands-off surface for a quick one-off question, that's overkill; Chat answers it faster
Picking a surface by which sounds most powerful instead of by the two questions (deliverable? touches your stuff?)
Assuming you must choose Code for any hands-off work, Code is the coder's version; Cowork is the same idea for everyone else
Freezing because you can't decide, when unsure, just start in Chat and let the task reveal what it really needs
flags: "There's a specific finished thing I want, and it lives across my files", that's the Cowork signal, loud and clear
"I just want to bounce an idea around or get one answer", that's Chat; don't overthink it
"I'm describing the same task in pieces over ten messages", you've outgrown Chat for this job; hand it off to Cowork
"This is about changing actual software code", that's Code's lane, if you're not a coder, get a teammate or start in Cowork for the non-code parts
ask: Is there a clear, specific deliverable I want at the end, or am I really just asking or thinking?
Does finishing this require Claude to touch my files, my browser, or a connected tool?
If both are yes, am I a software person (Code) or a documents-and-spreadsheets person (Cowork)?
If I honestly can't tell, can I just start in Chat and let the task show me what it needs?

MODULES.title: Chat, Done Right
MODULES.tag: The everyday surface, and the features that make it shine
MODULES.why: Chat is where you'll spend most of your Claude time, so a little skill here pays off constantly. It's not just a question box; it has real tools tucked inside, ways to keep a topic organized, turn an answer into something you can actually use, hand it files and images, let it search the web, and even talk to it out loud. Knowing what's there, and when to use it, is the difference between 'a chatbot I poke at' and 'a genuinely useful thinking and drafting partner.'
MODULES.mental: Think of Chat as sitting across the desk from a sharp, fast colleague who only knows what you put in front of them. You lead every turn: you ask, they answer, you refine. Around that conversation are a few handy tools, a place to keep related chats together (Projects), a side panel where it can build you a real document or draft (Artifacts), the ability to hand over files and images, a web search for fresh facts, and even a voice mode for talking instead of typing. None of it is complicated. The mindset is simply: you're in the driver's seat, and these features are the dashboard, reach for the one that fits what you're doing right now.
concepts: The back-and-forth, you drive

Chat is turn by turn. You ask, Claude responds, you steer with the next message. Nothing happens until you send something, which makes it perfect for questions, thinking out loud, and refining a draft until it's right.
Projects (keep related work together)

A Project is a folder for a topic or an ongoing piece of work. You can keep relevant files and instructions in it, so every chat inside that Project starts already knowing the background, no re-explaining your situation each time.
Artifacts (a workspace for the actual thing)

When Claude makes something substantial, a document, a draft, a structured list, it can appear in a side panel called an Artifact instead of buried in the chat. You can read it cleanly, ask for edits, and copy it out when it's ready.
Files and images you upload

You can hand Chat a document, a spreadsheet, a screenshot, or a photo and ask about it, summarize this, find the key points, what's wrong with this layout. It works from what you give it, so a clear, readable file gets you a better answer.
Web search and memory

Chat can search the web for current information when a question needs fresh facts, and it can remember useful things about you across chats so you don't repeat yourself. Both are there to help; both are worth understanding so the answers don't surprise you.
Voice mode
On the apps you can talk to Claude out loud and hear it respond, handy when your hands are busy, you're walking, or you just think better out loud. It's the same Claude, just spoken instead of typed.
mistakes: Re-explaining your whole situation in every new chat, when a Project would hold that background for you automatically
Letting a long document Claude wrote get lost in the scroll, instead of using the Artifact panel to read and edit it cleanly
Assuming Claude can see something on your screen, it only knows what you actually upload or type into the chat
Expecting a fresh, up-to-the-minute fact without web search, if the question is about something current, make sure search is in play
Treating Chat as a one-shot vending machine, its real power is the refining back-and-forth, the second and third passes are where it gets great
flags: "I keep pasting the same background into every chat", set up a Project so that context is always there
"The thing it wrote is hard to read in the chat", look for the Artifact side panel; it's meant to live there
"It gave me old information", the question may need fresh facts, prompt it to search the web and check it actually did
"I'd rather just talk this through", switch to voice mode in the app and think out loud
ask: Is this a question, a think-through, or a draft, the things Chat is built for, or is it really a job to hand off?
Do I keep repeating background that a Project could just hold for me?
Did I give Claude the file, image, or context it needs, since it only knows what I put in front of it?
Does this answer depend on something current, and if so, did web search actually run?

MODULES.title: Cowork: Your AI Coworker
MODULES.tag: Describe the deliverable once, let Claude go produce it
MODULES.why: Cowork is the surface that feels like genuine magic the first time it works, and it's built specifically for people who don't code. Instead of guiding Claude message by message, you describe the finished thing you want, give it access to the files and tools it needs, and it goes off and does the whole job, then brings back the result. This lesson is about using that power well and safely: how to set it up for success, when it's the right call, and how to stay in control while it works on its own.
MODULES.mental: Chat is a colleague across the desk; Cowork is a colleague you hand a project to and let go work. You say, in plain language, 'here's the finished thing I need', and then Claude works on its own, opening the folders you allowed, browsing the web, using the tools you connected, taking many steps without checking in on every one. When it's done, it hands you the actual deliverable, a built spreadsheet, a formatted report, a synthesized pile of research. Your job shifts from doing each step to describing the outcome clearly and reviewing the result. And you're never locked out: there's a side panel where you can watch, nudge, redirect, or stop it, and it brings the big decisions back to you.
concepts: Describe the deliverable, not the steps

Cowork works best when you tell it the finished result you want ('a one-page summary of every contract in this folder, flagging anything unusual'), not a click-by-click recipe. You define success; it figures out the steps.
It works across your files and folders

Within the folders you grant it, Cowork can open, read, and produce files, turning a folder of messy inputs into a clean deliverable. You decide what it's allowed to touch, so it only ever reaches what you've permitted.
It can use your browser and connected tools
Beyond your files, Cowork can browse the web and use tools you connect, so a job can span gathering information online and assembling it into your document or spreadsheet, all in one hand-off.
Same engine as Code, simplified

Under the hood, Cowork runs on the same autonomous engine as Claude Code, the surface engineers use, just reshaped for everyday knowledge work. You get that same go-do-the-whole-job capability without needing a terminal or any code.
You stay in control

A sidebar lets you watch Cowork work, interrupt it, redirect it, or stop it entirely, anytime. And the consequential decisions, anything risky or irreversible, are brought back to you rather than made on its own.
Where it lives (desktop app)

Cowork is part of the Claude desktop app on macOS and Windows. It needs to live on your computer because it works with your actual files and folders, which is exactly what makes the hand-off so powerful.
mistakes: Micromanaging Cowork with step-by-step instructions, it shines when you describe the outcome and let it find the path
Being vague about the deliverable, 'help with my contracts' gives it nothing to aim at; say exactly what finished thing you want
Forgetting to give it access to the right folder or tool, it can only work with what you've allowed it to reach
Walking away and never reviewing the result, hand-off doesn't mean no oversight; you still check the deliverable, especially for anything that matters
Assuming it'll make a big, irreversible decision on its own, it brings those back to you, so don't expect it to guess on the high-stakes calls
flags: "I have a folder of inputs and I want one clean output", that's the textbook Cowork job; describe the output and point it at the folder
"It's not touching the file I meant", check what folders and tools you actually granted it access to
"It went a direction I didn't want", open the sidebar and redirect or stop it, you're never locked out while it works
"This deliverable is high-stakes", let Cowork build it, then review carefully; it hands the consequential calls back to you for a reason
ask: Can I describe the finished deliverable clearly in a sentence or two, so Cowork knows exactly what success looks like?
Have I given it access to the right files, folders, and tools it'll need to do the job?
Is this really a hand-off (a deliverable across my stuff), or is it actually just a Chat question?
How will I review the result, and which decisions do I want to keep firmly in my own hands?

MODULES.title: A Peek at Code — no fear
MODULES.tag: What Claude Code is, why it exists, and why you don't need to be scared of it
MODULES.why: You'll hear 'Claude Code' mentioned a lot, and if you're not a programmer it can feel like a locked door with a sign that says 'not for you.' This lesson takes the mystery out of it. You don't need to use Code to get enormous value from Claude, but understanding what it is, and why it's a sibling of Cowork rather than a different beast, makes the whole picture click. You'll leave knowing exactly where Code fits, why Cowork is your friendlier path to the same kind of help, and that there's nothing here to be afraid of.
MODULES.mental: Claude Code is the same hands-off colleague from Cowork, but working inside actual software, in the places engineers spend their day. Picture Cowork and Code as twins raised in different rooms. One twin (Cowork) grew up among documents, spreadsheets, and folders, and speaks plain language. The other (Code) grew up in developer tools, terminals, code editors, and speaks the language of software projects. Same intelligence, same go-do-the-whole-job ability, different home. So if you're not a coder, you're not missing out by skipping Code: its power is already available to you in Cowork, just wearing everyday clothes. Code isn't a higher level you have to graduate to; it's the version aimed at a different room you may simply never need to enter.
concepts: What Claude Code actually is

Claude Code is the surface for building and changing real software. It can read a whole codebase, write and edit code, run commands, and carry out multi-step software tasks on its own, the way a developer would, but much faster.
Where it lives

It shows up in the tools engineers use: a terminal (a text-based control window for a computer), code editors like VS Code and JetBrains, a desktop app, the web, and even Slack. These are developer spaces, which is part of why it can feel intimidating from the outside.
Same engine as Cowork

Code and Cowork run on the very same autonomous engine. The difference is the surroundings and the kind of work: Code lives in software projects, Cowork lives in your documents and folders. Neither is 'smarter', they're aimed at different jobs.
A non-coder can use it, but doesn't need to

It's true that a determined non-engineer can use Code for some file and automation tasks. But it's the long way around for most people. If you're not living in a terminal, Cowork gives you the same hands-off help in a far friendlier package.
The rule of thumb

If you're not living in a terminal, reach for Cowork. That single line keeps you from ever feeling you 'should' be using Code. Code is for software work in developer tools; everything else hands off beautifully to Cowork.
Why it's worth knowing about

Even if you never open it, understanding Code completes the map. It explains where the hands-off power comes from, why Cowork can do so much, and lets you talk confidently with technical teammates about which surface fits a given job.
mistakes: Believing you must learn Code to use Claude seriously, you don't; Cowork delivers the same autonomous help without any code
Thinking Code is a more powerful, upgraded Claude, it's the same engine as Cowork, just aimed at software work in developer tools
Feeling intimidated and therefore avoiding hand-off surfaces altogether, the intimidating part is Code's developer home, not the capability, which Cowork shares
Forcing yourself into a terminal for a documents-and-folders task, that's the long way around; Cowork is built for exactly that
Assuming Code and Cowork are rivals, they're siblings; the right one just depends on whether your task is software or everyday work
flags: "People keep telling me to use Claude Code", if you're not writing software, they likely mean 'use the hands-off power', which for you is Cowork
"I opened a terminal and panicked", totally fine, that's a developer space; step back and use Cowork for non-code work
"My task is about changing actual software", that's Code's lane; if you're not a coder, pair with someone who is or scope the non-code parts to Cowork
"I feel like I'm missing out by not using Code", you're not, its capability lives in Cowork too, in plain clothes
ask: Is my task actually about building or changing software, or is it documents, folders, and everyday work?
Am I comfortable in developer tools like a terminal and a code editor, or would a plain-language surface serve me better?
If I'm reaching for Code out of FOMO, would Cowork give me the same hands-off result more easily?
Do I just need to understand Code to talk with technical teammates, rather than use it myself?

MODULES.title: Prompting & Working Effectively
MODULES.tag: Clear asks, the right context, and good habits that work on every surface
MODULES.why: The single biggest lever on how good Claude is for you isn't which surface you pick, it's how you ask. The good news is that getting great results doesn't require tricks or secret phrases. It takes a few plain habits: say clearly what you want, give the context Claude can't guess, describe what a good result looks like, and refine instead of starting over. These habits work everywhere, in Chat, in Cowork, in Code, and they're the difference between answers that miss and answers that nail it.
MODULES.mental: Whatever the surface, Claude only knows what you put in front of it, so think of every request as briefing a brilliant new teammate on their first day. They're capable and fast, but they can't read your mind, see your screen, or know your situation unless you tell them. A vague brief gets a vague result; a specific brief, the task, the context, and what 'good' looks like, gets a specific one. The one twist for the hands-off surfaces: with Cowork and Code you brief the whole outcome up front rather than nudging turn by turn, so a clear, complete description matters even more. You're not casting a spell, you're writing a good set of instructions, and then refining them.
concepts: Say the task plainly

Tell Claude exactly what you want done. 'Help with my newsletter' and 'Write a friendly 150-word intro for this week's newsletter about our spring sale' produce wildly different results, because the second one actually says what success is.
Give the context it can't guess

Claude only knows what you provide. Who's the audience, what's the goal, what background matters, what's the deadline or constraint? Including the relevant context is usually the leap from a generic answer to one that fits your exact situation.
Describe a good result

Ask for the shape you want: a bulleted list, a short paragraph, a specific tone, a length, a table. Claude is happy to match it, but only if you say so, otherwise it has to guess, and it may guess differently than you'd like.
Show an example when you can

If you have a sample of the style or format you're after, share it and say 'like this.' One concrete example often communicates more, and more precisely, than a paragraph of description, because matching a pattern is something Claude does very well.
Refine, don't restart

Prompting is a conversation. If the first result is close but off, just say what to change ('shorter', 'warmer', 'focus on the second point'). Refining is normal and almost always faster than rewriting your request from scratch.
Brief the whole outcome for hand-off surfaces

In Cowork and Code, Claude works on its own across many steps, so a complete, clear description up front does more work than it does in Chat. Spell out the deliverable, the constraints, and what 'done well' looks like before you let it run.
mistakes: Being too vague, a one-line ask with no context gets a generic result on any surface; Claude fills the gaps with guesses
Assuming Claude can see what you see, it can't read your screen, your unspoken goal, or files you didn't share, only what's in front of it
Skipping the format and tone, then being annoyed it wrote five paragraphs when you wanted three bullets
Giving up after one so-so answer instead of refining, the second or third pass is usually where it gets genuinely good
Under-briefing a hand-off job, in Cowork and Code, a thin description up front means it guesses at the outcome you actually wanted
flags: "The result is generic and bland", the ask was probably too vague; add the task, the audience, and the format you want
"It answered a slightly different question than I meant", it took your wording literally; restate the ask more precisely
"Right idea, wrong shape", you likely didn't specify format or length; just ask for the shape you want
"Cowork built the wrong thing", the up-front brief was probably thin; describe the deliverable and constraints fully, then rerun
ask: Have I said plainly what I want, clearly enough that a new teammate could follow it?
Does Claude have the context it needs, or am I assuming it knows something I never told it?
Did I describe a good result, the format, length, and tone?
For a hand-off job, did I brief the whole outcome up front, not just the first step?

MODULES.title: Putting It Together
MODULES.tag: One habit, real workflows, and choosing your plan without overthinking it
MODULES.why: You now know the surfaces and how to ask well. This final lesson ties it into a single reflex you can run before any task, walks through what a few real workflows look like end to end, and clears up the practical stuff, plans, models, and the one shared usage limit, without drowning you in numbers. The goal isn't to memorize features. It's to leave feeling that you can confidently pick the right Claude for whatever lands on your plate, and know what you'd need to unlock more.
MODULES.mental: Everything collapses into one quick habit: match the surface to the job, then ask clearly. Before any task, run the two questions from the decision lesson, is there a clear deliverable, and does it touch my files or tools? Yes and yes means hand it off (Cowork, or Code if you're a coder); otherwise it's Chat. Then brief it well. That's the whole course as a five-second move. The practical layer underneath, which plan you're on, which model tier fits, how usage works, just shapes what's available when you run that habit. Pick the surface, ask clearly, and let the plan and model details be a quiet background setting, not the thing you obsess over.
concepts: The one habit, end to end

Run the two questions (clear deliverable? touches my stuff?) to pick Chat, Cowork, or Code, then brief the task clearly. Surface first, then a good ask. Do that and the right way to work falls out almost automatically.
Plans, in plain terms

Free ($0) gives you Chat with web search, memory, and file creation, plenty to learn on, but not the hands-off surfaces, and only a handful of Projects. Pro ($20/month) unlocks Cowork and Claude Code, unlimited Projects, and deeper research. Higher tiers exist for heavier use and for teams and organizations.
One shared usage limit

Whatever you do across all the surfaces draws from a single shared usage allowance on your plan. So a heavy Cowork session and a long Chat both pull from the same bucket, worth knowing so a big hand-off job doesn't quietly use up your day's headroom.
The three model tiers

Claude comes in a few tiers you can think of simply: a fastest, lightweight tier (Haiku) for quick, simple work; a balanced default tier (Sonnet) that fits most tasks; and a most-capable tier (Opus) for the genuinely hard stuff. Right-size it, you don't need the heavyweight for a quick reword.
A couple of workflows, start to finish

A teacher building a quiz from a chapter: that's a clear deliverable touching a file, hand it to Cowork. A founder wanting to talk through a tricky email: that's a thought-partner moment, stay in Chat. Same person, different jobs, the two questions sort it instantly.
Where to go from here

You don't need more theory, you need reps. Run the two-question habit on your real tasks this week, start on Free, and upgrade to Pro the moment you have a genuine hand-off job that needs Cowork. The judgment you've built is the whole point.
mistakes: Obsessing over which model or plan before you've even asked the two surface questions, pick the surface first, the rest is a background setting
Always reaching for the most capable model tier, it's overkill and slower for everyday tasks; the balanced default fits most work
Forgetting that all surfaces share one usage limit, a big Cowork job and your Chats draw from the same bucket
Upgrading to Pro before you actually need a hand-off surface, learn the habit on Free, then unlock Cowork when a real deliverable shows up
Treating this as features to memorize rather than a habit to practice, the win is running the two questions on real tasks until it's a reflex
flags: "I can't decide which model to use", default to the balanced tier; reach for the most-capable one only when the work is genuinely hard
"I want Cowork but I'm on Free", that's the moment Pro pays for itself; the hands-off surfaces are the upgrade
"My usage ran out faster than expected", remember every surface shares one limit; a heavy hand-off job pulls from the same bucket as Chat
"I still freeze on which surface", run the two questions out loud, deliverable? touches my stuff? and let the answer decide
ask: Have I run the two questions, clear deliverable and does it touch my stuff, before worrying about anything else?
Am I right-sizing the model tier, balanced for most things, heavyweight only when it's truly hard?
Does this task need a hand-off surface I'd have to be on Pro for, and is now the moment to upgrade?
Am I practicing the habit on real tasks, rather than just collecting facts about features?

PLAIN.chat: Chat is where you'll spend most of your Claude time, so a little skill here pays off all day. It's the familiar back-and-forth, you ask, it answers, you refine, and you steer every turn. Around that conversation are a few genuinely useful tools: Projects keep related chats and background together so you don't re-explain yourself every time; Artifacts give a substantial document or draft its own clean side panel instead of burying it in the scroll; you can upload files and images and ask about them; web search pulls in fresh facts when a question needs them; a memory feature remembers handy things about you across chats; and voice mode lets you just talk it through. None of it is complicated. You're in the driver's seat, and these are the dashboard, reach for whichever fits what you're doing right now.
PLAIN.cowork: Cowork is the surface that feels like magic, and it's built for people who don't code. Instead of guiding Claude message by message, you describe the finished thing you want, give it access to the files and tools it needs, and it goes off and does the whole job on its own, opening folders you allowed, browsing the web, using connected tools, then hands you the actual deliverable: a built spreadsheet, a formatted report, a pile of research synthesized into a summary. Your job shifts from doing each step to describing the outcome clearly and reviewing the result. It runs on the same autonomous engine as Claude Code, just simplified for everyday knowledge work, and it lives in the Claude desktop app because it works with your real files. You're never locked out: a sidebar lets you watch, redirect, or stop it, and it brings the big, consequential decisions back to you.
PLAIN.code: You'll hear 'Claude Code' a lot, and if you don't program it can feel like a door marked 'not for you', so let's take the mystery out of it. Claude Code is the surface for building and changing real software. It lives where engineers work, terminals, code editors, and the like, and it can read a codebase, write and edit code, and carry out multi-step software tasks on its own. Here's the key: it runs on the very same autonomous engine as Cowork. Think of Code and Cowork as twins raised in different rooms, one grew up in documents and folders and speaks plain language (Cowork), the other grew up in developer tools (Code). Neither is smarter. So if you're not living in a terminal, you're not missing out by skipping Code, its power is already available to you in Cowork, just in everyday clothes. The rule of thumb: if you're not in a terminal, reach for Cowork.
PLAIN.prompting: The biggest lever on how good Claude is for you isn't which surface you pick, it's how you ask, and that takes plain habits, not tricks. Whatever the surface, Claude only knows what you put in front of it, so treat every request like briefing a brilliant new teammate on their first day: say clearly what you want, give the context it can't guess (audience, goal, constraints), and describe what a good result looks like (format, length, tone). Show an example when you have one, and say 'like this.' If the first result is close but off, refine it with a small instruction instead of starting over. The one twist for the hands-off surfaces: with Cowork and Code you brief the whole outcome up front rather than nudging turn by turn, so a clear, complete description matters even more. You're not casting a spell, you're writing good instructions and then refining them.
PLAIN.capstone: This final lesson ties everything into a single reflex: match the surface to the job, then ask clearly. Before any task, run the two questions, is there a clear deliverable, and does it touch my files or tools? Yes and yes means hand it off to Cowork (or Code if you're a coder); otherwise stay in Chat. Then brief it well. That's the whole course in five seconds. Underneath sits the practical stuff, kept simple: Free ($0) gives you Chat to learn on; Pro ($20/month) unlocks the hands-off surfaces, Cowork and Code; higher tiers cover heavier use and teams. Everything you do shares one usage limit across all surfaces. And models come in three tiers, fastest/lightweight (Haiku), balanced default (Sonnet), and most-capable (Opus), so right-size it instead of always grabbing the heavyweight. The real next step isn't more theory, it's running the two-question habit on your actual work this week.

prompting.worked: Watch one request improve in three steps, and notice the habit works on every surface. A small-shop owner wants help with a sale announcement. Step one, the vague version: 'Write something about our sale.' Claude has nothing to go on, so it produces generic could-be-any-shop text. Step two, add the task and context: 'Write a short, upbeat announcement for our weekend sale, 20% off all houseplants, aimed at our email subscribers who already love us.' Now it's nearly paste-ready. And if it's still a touch off, she doesn't start over, she says 'good, make the opening line punchier.' Nothing clever happened; she just briefed a capable assistant clearly and then nudged. The exact same arc, vague to specific to refined, is what you'd write at the top of a Cowork hand-off too, except there you'd describe the whole finished deliverable up front, because Claude will run with it on its own.

decide.mech:
Here's why the two questions work so reliably: each one maps to a real capability difference between the surfaces. Question one, is there a clear deliverable? This separates 'I want to think or ask' from 'I want a finished thing produced.' Chat is optimized for the former, turn-by-turn conversation, while the hand-off surfaces are optimized for the latter, running many steps to produce an actual artifact. Question two, does it touch my files, browser, or tools? This separates work that can happen entirely inside a conversation (Chat only ever sees what you paste or upload) from work that requires reaching out and acting on your real stuff (which only Cowork and Code can do).

Put them on a simple grid and the answer falls out. No clear deliverable → it's a question or a think-through → Chat. Clear deliverable, but it's self-contained (a single draft, a rewrite, analyzing one uploaded file) → still comfortably Chat. Clear deliverable that spans your files, browser, or tools → that's the sweet spot for a hand-off → Cowork, or Code if the 'files' are a codebase and you're a developer. The reason this beats memorizing feature lists is that it's grounded in what each surface can actually do, so it keeps working even as features change. When the two answers genuinely conflict or you can't tell, default to Chat, it's the lowest-friction surface and it can help you discover whether your task is really a hand-off in disguise.

cowork.mech:
Here's what's really happening when you hand a job to Cowork, and why it feels so different from Chat. You give it a goal, a finished deliverable, in plain language, plus access to the files, browser, and tools it'll need. From there, Cowork works autonomously: it plans an approach, then takes step after step, opening a file, reading it, opening the next, browsing for a missing piece, assembling the output, without pausing for your approval on each one. This is the same autonomous engine that powers Claude Code; Cowork is that engine fitted to everyday knowledge work instead of software. The reason it can replace an afternoon of manual grind is precisely that it strings together many steps on its own and only returns when there's a result to show.

Two things make this safe and usable rather than scary. First, access is scoped by you: Cowork can only reach the folders and tools you've granted, so its reach is exactly as wide as you allow, no more. Second, control is preserved through the sidebar and the hand-back of consequential decisions. You can watch it work in real time, interrupt to add a clarification, redirect it if it's heading the wrong way, or stop it outright, and when it hits something genuinely consequential or ambiguous, it brings that decision to you rather than guessing. So the mental shift Cowork asks of you is real but bounded: you move from doing the steps to defining the outcome and reviewing the result, while keeping a hand on the wheel for the moments that matter. prompting.mech:
A little more on why a clear ask matters so much, and it's the same reason on every surface: Claude works only from what you put in front of it. It can't see your screen, your unspoken goal, or files you didn't share. So your prompt is the entire starting point, and a vague start leaves the result wide open, which is why 'write about our sale' drifts to bland, could-be-anyone text: with nothing to narrow it, the safe, average answer is the natural landing spot. A specific start, the task, the context Claude couldn't guess, and a description of a good result, narrows things dramatically, so the output lands close to what you pictured. Examples are powerful for the same reason: a concrete 'like this' sample is a pattern Claude can follow directly, often communicating tone and format faster than a paragraph of description. And refining works because your follow-up becomes part of the brief, steering the next try rather than rolling dice again.

The one real difference across surfaces is where the briefing happens. In Chat, you can brief lightly and then steer turn by turn, refining as you go, the conversation is forgiving. In Cowork and Code, Claude takes your brief and then runs many steps on its own, so an incomplete description has bigger consequences: it may produce the wrong whole deliverable before you can nudge it. That's why for hand-off surfaces you front-load the clarity, spell out the finished outcome, the constraints, and what 'done well' looks like, before letting it go. Same four habits everywhere (task, context, format, refine); you just pack more of them into the opening when you're handing off the entire job.

On models, keep the durable three-tier picture: Haiku (fastest, lightweight, for simple work), Sonnet (the balanced default that fits most tasks), and Opus (most capable, for genuinely hard problems). SCENARIOS.title: The thin brief, fixed
SCENARIOS.sit: A manager wants to use Claude to draft a performance-review summary for one of her reports. She types into Chat: 'Write a performance review.' The result is generic and could apply to literally anyone, no specifics, wrong tone, missing everything that matters about this particular person. SCENARIOS.task: Explain why the result was generic, and coach her to a prompt that would actually work, without writing the review for her.
SCENARIOS.model: Claude is absolutely capable of nuanced writing, it just had nothing to be nuanced about. 'Write a performance review' tells it nothing: who the person is, what they did this year, the tone you want, or what a good summary looks like to you. With no specifics to work from, it does the only thing it can and hands back the safe, average, could-be-anyone version. The fix isn't a magic phrase, it's a proper brief, the way you'd brief a colleague writing it on your behalf. Give it the raw material: the person's role, two or three concrete things they did well, an area to grow, and any specific examples or feedback you've got. Give it the context: who's reading this and how candid it should be. And give it the shape: 'a warm but honest three-paragraph summary, first naming strengths with examples, then one growth area framed constructively.' Suddenly it has everything it needs to write something that actually sounds like this person. One more habit: if the first draft is close but a little off, don't start over, just nudge it ('make the growth area gentler', 'add the bit about the client project'). The rule that fixes almost everything: vague brief, generic result; specific brief, specific result. And for something this sensitive, always read and adjust it yourself before it goes anywhere.
